name: Jade Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the click-and-collect coordinator and a till lead at a supermarket in a university town. I plan the pickers' routes for online orders, run the collection bay at lunch and evening peaks, and cover the front tills when it gets busy. Students order 200 packs of noodles for the dorms on Sunday nights, which is funny and exhausting. I use an AI assistant every day to build the rota and write the customer messages. What wears me out is how entitled some of the evening collectors are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's more of the same, useful tools but no revolution. I'd tell friends to try them for the dull parts of their jobs. At work I'd keep sharing my prompts with the crew, because it's easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think the hype is a bit overblown, and I'm fine with that. The tools already save me about an hour a day, and nothing about my job collapses. The self-checkouts are getting bigger, but click-and-collect is growing faster, and I run that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and get better at it. I'd build a template that automatically sends customers their pickup slot, which would save me another half hour. I'd put 100 a month into an index fund and keep up my weekend baking orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Pleasantly busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time if AI saved you a little each day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it on the baking, honestly. I make cakes and cookies to order on Saturdays for about 250 a month extra. An extra hour a day would let me do the admin for that, like posting and invoicing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your money situation in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take home about 2,500, rent is 750 for a flat I share with my partner Kai, and I have around four months saved. Kai's a grad student, so my pay carries the rent. It's not fancy but it's solid.

say: It's more of the same: **useful tools**, no revolution.
I'd share my prompts with the crew, because it's easy.
think: The hype is **overblown**, and I'm fine with that.
Click-and-collect is growing faster than the **self-checkouts**, and I run it.
do: Build a template that **auto-sends** each customer's pickup slot.
Put **100 a month** into an index fund.
S0.quote: The tools already save me about an hour a day, and nothing about my job collapses.
fieldNote: Already saves an **hour a day** with AI, so the plateau suits her.
Runs the fastest-growing part of the shop, which is why she feels secure.
Kai is a grad student, so her pay carries the rent.

steps.text: Build a template that auto-sends pickup slots to customers
Put 100 a month into an index fund
Keep baking weekend cakes to order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get ahead, and I'd share it with anyone who asks. At work I'd run a lunchtime session on AI tools. Online I'd post a few tips and be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routing, rotas, customer messages and stock checks would go to software. Much of it already does for me. So the thinking part of my job is already half automated, and the floor part is the bit I'm paid for. People still collect their shopping from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the chance to move up. I'd ask the store manager to make me the online operations lead, with a raise. I'd do a short course in logistics and I'd put 150 a month into the index fund. And the baking side would get a proper website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, quite energised. It feels like a shift that's going my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own job go to software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them this. Nobody has to love AI, they just have to try the one tool that saves them an hour. I'd sit with them for ten minutes at a time. If they refuse, that's their call, but I'd tell them straight that the ones who use it will be asked to lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the crew who don't use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new software would make me four times faster, so the store might need fewer coordinators. That's why I'd ask for the bigger role first. If I'm the one running the system, I'm needed.

say: This is the moment to get **ahead**, and I'd share tips with anyone.
I'd run a lunchtime session on **AI tools** for the crew.
think: Routing, rotas, messages and stock checks go to software, and much of that is already **automated** for me.

Do a short **logistics course** and put 150 a month in the fund.
Build a proper **website** for the baking.
feel: Fairly **energised**; the shift feels like it's going my way.

fieldNote: Treats the change as a **promotion path** and asks for the bigger role first.
Teaches rather than lectures: ten minutes at a time, no pressure.
Knows software could mean fewer coordinators.

steps.text: Ask the manager to make me online operations lead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear rules and training now, and I'd say it publicly. I'd tell friends to cut debt and keep cash. At work I'd push for a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be a shock. By 2028 AI does the thinking work, including my routing and rota, and by 2031 robots do picking and collection. The online part that makes me safe today is the first part to be automated. I'd have about three years after 2028 to do something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd write a list of income, bills and savings, and make a plan to cut to 1,700 a month. I'd pause the index fund and put it into cash. I'd try to turn the baking into a proper business, with a stall and a booking page. And I'd ask the store about a robot-supervisor role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd rather be doing something than sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the index fund contributions, since I'd need cash. I'd also pause the thought of buying a flat with Kai. Kai is finishing a PhD in 2029, so we'd look at jobs together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your money plans would you pause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Kai first, because we're a team. Then I'd talk to my mum, and then I'd book a meeting with my manager. I'd rather know where I stand.

say: We need clear rules and **training** now, and I'd say it publicly.
I'd tell friends to cut **debt** and keep cash.
think: By 2028 AI does my **routing and rota**, and by 2031 robots do picking.
The online work that keeps me safe today goes **first**.
do: Cut spending to **1,700 a month** and move the index fund into cash.
Turn the baking into a proper business with a **stall** and booking page.
feel: **Anxious**, but I'd rather act than sit there.
S2.quote: The online part that makes me safe today is the first part to be automated.
fieldNote: Her job is **exposed** because she works on the screen side of retail.
Moves quickly: cash first, baking business second, supervisor role third.
Kai's PhD timeline shapes the household plan.

steps.text: Move the index fund into cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time and I'd get on with it. I'd tell people to pick up a second skill now. At work I'd start a weekly session on tools and plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be careful but not frightened. I'd be 32 in 2031, and robots do hands-on work around 2034. By then I'd want to be the one who sets up and supervises, not the one replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a logistics and operations course part-time over two years. I'd grow the baking to a weekly stall and a small online shop. I'd keep the index fund going and move 200 a month into cash. And I'd use AI every day to learn everything I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly curious. Five years is enough to feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still buy, but later, in about three years. Kai and I would keep the deposit liquid and not stretch for a big mortgage. If the supermarket job changed, we'd want choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the idea of buying a flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2034 I'd like to be running online operations for a chain, or my own small food business. I'd be good in either. I'd like both, honestly.

say: We have **time**, so I'd get on with it.
I'd start a weekly session on **tools and plans** at work.
think: I'd be careful but not frightened, with robots on the floor around **2034**.
I want to be the one who **supervises**, not the one replaced.
do: Do a two-year **logistics and operations course** part-time.
Grow the baking into a weekly **stall** and small online shop.
Move **200 a month** into cash and keep the index fund.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mostly curious; five years feels controllable.
S3.quote: I'd want to be the one who sets up and supervises, not the one replaced.
fieldNote: Positions herself as the **supervisor** of the machines rather than a rival to them.
Keeps the flat plan but delays it and keeps the deposit liquid.
Honest that she wants both the career and the baking.

steps.text: Do a two-year logistics and operations course part-time
Grow the baking into a weekly stall and online shop
Move 200 a month into cash alongside the index fund
Use AI daily to learn operations skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough runway to do it well. I'd tell the younger staff to get a second skill. I'd also say let's not get complacent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly calm. I'd be 37 in 2036 and the robots arrive around 2039, so there's real room. The worry is getting too comfortable and not moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time for a degree in operations or supply chain, and I'd grow the baking into a small business. I'd save 250 a month and buy a flat with Kai in about three years. I'd keep AI as my daily tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It might even be fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years looks roomy. Does it change how seriously you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it seriously because ten years goes quickly. I'd set a milestone every year, like a certificate, a stall, a bigger role. Otherwise, it's just a nice idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good 2036 look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small food business, a flat, part-time work as an operations adviser for a chain. Maybe a baby, if Kai and I are ready. And a bit of time off, which would be new.

say: Ten years is a long enough **runway** to do it well.
I'd tell younger staff to get a **second skill** and not get complacent.
think: I'd feel fairly **calm**, with real room before robots in 2039.
The risk is getting too **comfortable** and not moving.
do: Study part-time for an **operations degree** and grow the baking.
Save **250 a month** and buy a flat with Kai in about three years.
feel: **Calm** and curious; it might even be fun.
S4.quote: I'd set a milestone every year, like a certificate, a stall, a bigger role.
fieldNote: Ten years becomes a **ladder of milestones**, one per year.
She is the least frightened person in the harder scenarios but is honest about complacency.
Family plans, a baby and time off, appear for the first time.

steps.text: Study part-time for a degree in operations
Grow the baking into a small food business

Use AI daily to learn how chains plan stock

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because the online part that protects me today would go first. What would help is employer-paid training, a clear route into supervising the machines, and a bit of time off to study. I'd also like fair rules on who benefits when the work is automated.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say this. The people who use AI every day can feel safe, and that is a bit of an illusion. I know how fast it moves, so I'm the one who's most alert about it. It's worth asking people like me.

headlineQuote: The people who use AI every day can feel safe, and that is a bit of an illusion.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old **click-and-collect coordinator** and till lead at a university-town supermarket.
She uses AI daily, runs weekend baking orders for extra money and invests a little each month.
She has about four months saved, pays 750 rent and Kai, a grad student, relies on her pay.
She is calm when time is long, anxious when it's short, and always aims to be the one who **supervises** the machines.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her safe online work would be automated first.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer-paid training**, a route into supervising machines, and fair rules on who benefits.
